lesson.title: CUBIC: Reshaping the Sawtooth for Fast, Long Links
lesson.summary: TCP CUBIC, the default congestion control algorithm on Linux, replaces Reno's straight-line additive increase with a cubic growth curve that recovers window size quickly after a loss and probes more aggressively for bandwidth on high-capacity, high-delay links.
lesson.body:
TCP Reno's additive increase does its job well on modest, low-delay connections, but it runs into a real limitation on what are often called long fat networks, links with both high bandwidth and high round trip time, such as intercontinental fiber paths. Because Reno adds only about one segment per round trip regardless of how large the window already is, and because higher RTT means fewer round trips occur per second, Reno's growth rate after a loss is inversely tied to RTT: a connection with a long RTT takes a very long time to climb back to a large window after any cutback, leaving substantial bandwidth unused for extended periods. This was a known and increasingly costly weakness of pure AIMD as network capacity grew.

CUBIC, which has been the default congestion control algorithm in Linux since kernel 2.6.19, addresses this by replacing the straight-line additive increase of congestion avoidance with a cubic function of the time elapsed since the last window reduction. The window grows according to a curve shaped like a cubic function: after a loss event cuts the window, growth is initially fast, then flattens out as the window approaches Wmax, the window size at which the previous loss occurred, then accelerates again if no further loss occurs, probing past the old ceiling in search of newly available capacity. This concave-then-convex shape is the defining feature of CUBIC and the source of its name.

The behavior is deliberately designed around Wmax rather than around the clock in round trips. Right after a cutback, CUBIC grows quickly because the sender is confident it is well below the network's actual capacity, having just backed off from it. As the window approaches Wmax, growth slows almost to a plateau, since the network showed congestion at roughly that point last time and a cautious approach reduces the chance of an immediate repeat loss. If the window reaches and holds near Wmax without triggering loss, that is new information suggesting the network can now sustain more, perhaps because competing traffic has left, so CUBIC's convex phase begins accelerating growth again to probe for that additional capacity. Crucially, this growth curve is a function of real time elapsed, not of round trips completed, which means CUBIC's growth rate does not shrink as RTT grows the way Reno's does. This makes CUBIC substantially fairer to, and much faster on, connections with large round trip times, without penalizing short-RTT connections either.

Consider two connections sharing a bottleneck, one with a 10 millisecond RTT and one with a 200 millisecond RTT, both running plain Reno. The short-RTT connection completes far more round trips per second, so its one-segment-per-RTT additive increase accumulates window size roughly twenty times faster in wall-clock time, letting it dominate the shared link. Because CUBIC's growth function depends on elapsed time rather than RTT count, both connections following CUBIC increase their windows at comparable rates in real time after a loss, narrowing that imbalance considerably. CUBIC still reduces its window multiplicatively on loss, much like Reno, so it remains a loss-based algorithm at its core; what it changes is the shape of the recovery curve rather than the fundamental signal (packet loss) that triggers a cutback. That reliance on loss as the trigger is exactly what the next algorithm, TCP BBR, abandons in favor of an entirely different approach.
